questions.lo: Properties of solids, liquids and gases using the particle model
questions.q: Which state of matter has both a fixed shape and a fixed volume?
questions.explain: A solid keeps a fixed shape and a fixed volume because its particles are locked in a regular pattern and can only vibrate on the spot.

questions.lo: Arrangement, closeness and movement of particles in each state
questions.q: In which state are the particles arranged in a regular pattern, packed closely together and only vibrating?
options: They are the same in all states
questions.explain: In a solid the particles form a regular, ordered pattern, are touching, and vibrate about fixed positions without moving past one another.

questions.lo: Arrangement, closeness and movement of particles in each state
questions.q: Which statement best describes the particles in a gas?
options: Close together and vibrating on the spot
Far apart and moving quickly in random directions
Close together but sliding past each other
questions.explain: Gas particles are far apart with lots of empty space between them and move quickly in random directions, which is why a gas fills its container and can be squashed.

questions.lo: Properties of solids, liquids and gases using the particle model
questions.q: A substance has a fixed volume but takes the shape of its container. Which state is it?
questions.explain: A liquid keeps its volume (particles are still close together) but has no fixed shape, so it flows to take the shape of the container.

questions.lo: Properties of solids, liquids and gases using the particle model
questions.q: Why can a gas be squashed (compressed) into a smaller space but a liquid cannot?
options: Gas particles are smaller than liquid particles
There is a lot of empty space between gas particles, but liquid particles are already touching
questions.explain: In a gas the particles are far apart with empty space to be pushed into. In a liquid the particles are already close together and touching, so there is almost no space to compress.

questions.lo: Naming changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing, sublimation)
questions.q: What is the name of the change of state from a liquid to a solid?
questions.explain: Freezing is liquid to solid (for example water turning to ice). Melting is the reverse, solid to liquid.

questions.lo: Naming changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing, sublimation)
questions.q: Water droplets form on the inside of a cold window on a winter morning. What change of state is this?
questions.explain: Water vapour (a gas) in the air cools on the cold glass and turns into liquid droplets. Gas to liquid is condensing.

questions.lo: Naming changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing, sublimation)
questions.q: A puddle slowly dries up on a warm day, well below 100 degrees C, with the water turning to gas only from its surface. What is this process called?
questions.explain: Evaporation turns liquid into gas from the surface and can happen below the boiling point. Boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

questions.lo: Naming changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing, sublimation)
questions.q: Solid carbon dioxide (dry ice) turns straight into a gas without becoming a liquid first. What is this change called?
questions.explain: Sublimation is when a solid changes directly into a gas (or a gas directly into a solid) with no liquid stage in between.

questions.lo: Naming changes of state (melting, freezing, boiling, evaporating, condensing, sublimation)
questions.q: What is the key difference between boiling and evaporating?
options: Boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point; evaporating happens only from the surface and can occur below the boiling point
Boiling makes a solid; evaporating makes a gas
They are exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Both turn liquid into gas. Boiling occurs throughout the liquid at its boiling point, while evaporation occurs only at the surface and at any temperature below boiling.

questions.lo: Conservation of mass on a change of state
questions.q: A 30 g ice cube melts completely in a sealed, weighed tub. What is the mass of the water afterwards?
questions.explain: No particles are created or destroyed during a change of state, so mass is conserved. 30 g of ice becomes 30 g of water.

questions.lo: Conservation of mass on a change of state
questions.q: An open beaker of water is boiled and its mass on the balance goes down. What is the best explanation?
options: Mass is destroyed when water boils
Water particles escape into the air as a gas, so they are no longer on the balance
The particles get lighter when heated
questions.explain: Mass is not destroyed. The water particles escape as a gas into the air, so they leave the beaker. In a sealed container the mass would stay the same.

questions.lo: Gas pressure explained by particle collisions
questions.q: What causes the pressure of a gas on the walls of its container?
options: The particles resting against the walls
The gas particles colliding with the walls
questions.explain: Gas pressure is caused by the many collisions of fast-moving gas particles with the container walls. Each collision gives a tiny push, and billions of them add up.

questions.lo: Gas pressure explained by particle collisions
questions.q: A sealed can of gas is heated. What happens to the gas pressure inside, and why?
options: It falls, because particles slow down
It rises, because the particles move faster and hit the walls harder and more often
It stays the same, because heat does not change pressure
It rises, because the particles grow bigger
questions.explain: Heating gives the particles more energy so they move faster, striking the walls harder and more frequently, which increases the pressure.

questions.lo: Diffusion explained by random particle movement
options: Particles being pulled downwards by gravity
The spreading of particles from where they are crowded to where there are fewer, by random movement
questions.explain: Diffusion is the spreading of particles from a high concentration to a low concentration because the particles are moving randomly all the time.

questions.lo: Diffusion explained by random particle movement
questions.q: You can smell perfume across a room a short time after it is sprayed in one corner. Which idea explains this best?
options: The perfume solids diffuse through the walls
Gas particles from the perfume diffuse, spreading out by random movement
The particles melt and drip across the floor
Gravity carries the smell across the room
questions.explain: The perfume's gas particles move randomly and diffuse from the crowded corner across the room until they reach your nose.

questions.lo: Diffusion explained by random particle movement
questions.q: In which situation does diffusion happen fastest?
questions.explain: Diffusion is fastest in gases because gas particles move quickly and have plenty of empty space to travel through. It is slower in liquids and does not happen in solids.

questions.lo: Arrangement, closeness and movement of particles in each state
questions.q: A student writes: 'When ice melts, the particles themselves melt and get bigger.' Why is this wrong?
options: The particles do not melt or change size; only their arrangement and movement change
Nothing is wrong, it is correct
questions.explain: Individual particles never melt, grow or change. Melting is the particles gaining energy and moving apart from their fixed positions, while each particle stays exactly the same.
